faq.a: Stopping reduces muscle oxygen demand, allowing the limited arterial flow to meet metabolic needs.
faq.q: Why does walking relieve the pain quickly?

faq.a: No; in diabetes or renal disease arteries may be calcified and incompressible, giving a falsely high ABI.
faq.q: Can a normal ABI rule out PAD?

faq.a: Only when lifestyle measures fail and the disease is severe (Fontaine IIb or higher) or limb‑threatening.
faq.q: Is surgery always required for claudication?

exam: A 58‑year‑old smoker presents with calf pain after walking 150 m. Which bedside test confirms arterial disease and what threshold is diagnostic? — Ankle‑brachial index; ABI < 0.90 confirms PAD.
During a ward round you note absent pedal pulses but a normal ABI of 1.35. What explains this discrepancy and what test should you order? — Medial arterial calcification; obtain toe‑brachial index.

A patient with intermittent claudication asks about medication. Why is aspirin preferred over clopidogrel in this setting? — Aspirin is cheap, widely available, and has no interaction with common anti‑malaria drugs; clopidogrel adds cost without extra benefit for PAD alone.
You suspect neurogenic claudication. Which feature of the history differentiates it from arterial claudication? — Pain improves with lumbar flexion (sitting) and worsens with standing.
A 62‑year‑old diabetic has an ABI of 0.68 and a non‑healing foot ulcer. What is the next urgent step? — Refer for revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) to prevent limb loss.
Explain why supervised walking improves walking distance despite unchanged arterial stenosis. — Repeated exercise promotes collateral vessel development and improves muscle efficiency.
During a community clinic you cannot perform duplex ultrasound. How can you still assess severity of PAD? — Use post‑exercise ABI drop ≥0.20 or measure segmental pressures with a handheld Doppler.

A patient with Leriche syndrome presents with buttock claudication and erectile dysfunction. Which arterial segment is occluded and what additional assessment is needed? — Aorto‑iliac occlusion; assess for abdominal aortic aneurysm and cardiac risk.
ai.title: Intermittent Claudication
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Intermittent claudication is exercise‑induced leg pain caused by peripheral arterial disease. Diagnosis relies on history, pulse exam and simple bedside tests; management focuses on risk‑factor control and supervised exercise.

b: Ask: distance to pain onset, speed of relief, reproducibility on repeat walk
Check femoral, popliteal and pedal pulses; note any bruits
Ankle‑brachial index (ABI) <0.90 confirms arterial obstruction
sections.p: Intermittent claudication is reproducible leg pain that begins after a predictable walking distance and resolves within minutes of rest. It reflects insufficient blood flow to skeletal muscle during exertion.

b: Fontaine I: asymptomatic, ABI 0.90‑1.0
Fontaine IIa: pain after >200 m, ABI 0.70‑0.90
Fontaine IIb: pain after ≤200 m, ABI 0.40‑0.70
Fontaine III: rest pain, ABI <0.40
Fontaine IV: gangrene
sections.p: Severity is graded by walking distance and ABI. The Fontaine and Rutherford classifications are used worldwide.

b: Atherosclerotic disease (smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia)
Buerger disease (young male smokers, more common in East Africa)
Thrombo‑angiitis obliterans secondary to HIV or TB treatment
Fibromuscular dysplasia (rare, younger women)
Embolic occlusion from rheumatic heart disease or atrial fibrillation
sections.p: Atherosclerosis of the lower‑extremity arteries is the dominant cause, but in low‑resource settings other occlusive or inflammatory processes must be considered.

b: Pain pattern matches distance walked
Absent or diminished distal pulses
Skin may be thin, shiny, with hair loss
Coldness of foot compared with opposite side
sections.p: Patients report cramping or burning pain in calves, thighs or buttocks that forces them to stop walking. Pain is absent at rest and improves quickly when activity stops.

t.b: Is arterial flow reduced? – ABI <0.90 confirms PAD; >1.30 suggests non‑compressible vessels.
Is disease distal to the ankle? – Low toe‑brachial index (<0.70) indicates distal disease when ABI is unreliable.
Where is the lesion? – Shows flow velocities, stenosis severity, and plaque morphology; portable units are useful where CT angiography is unavailable.
What is functional limitation? – Distance to pain onset quantifies severity; repeat ABI after exercise can unmask mild disease.

t.a: Blood tests (lipid profile, HbA1c, renal function)
t.b: What are modifiable risk factors? – Guides secondary prevention; treat dyslipidaemia, diabetes, renal impairment.

t.a: If duplex unavailable: handheld Doppler with post‑exercise ABI
t.b: How to confirm disease without imaging? – Measure ABI before and after a 5‑minute walk; a drop ≥0.20 suggests PAD.

b: Rest pain (pain at night, especially when leg is elevated)
Non‑healing ulcer or gangrene
Sudden loss of pulse after trauma – possible acute embolus
New chest pain, dyspnoea or neurological deficit
sections.p: Unrecognised disease can progress to critical limb ischemia, ulceration, gangrene and amputation. Systemic atherosclerosis raises risk of myocardial infarction and stroke.

b: Smoking cessation – most powerful risk‑factor modification
Statin (e.g., atorvastatin) – lowers LDL, stabilises plaque; generic forms are affordable
Blood pressure control (ACE‑inhibitor or thiazide) – protects kidneys and vessels
Supervised walking programme – 30‑45 min, 3‑5 times/week improves distance by 30‑50 % without equipment
Structured exercise in community health centres when formal programmes unavailable
Revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) – reserved for Fontaine III/IV or disabling IIb; refer to tertiary centre
sections.p: Treat the atherosclerotic burden, improve collateral flow, and relieve symptoms. In low‑resource settings, lifestyle change and inexpensive drugs are the mainstay.

b: Check ABI and pulse exam every 6‑12 months
Re‑measure walking distance at each visit
Re‑assess lipid, glucose and blood pressure targets
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus – reduces cardiovascular events
sections.p: Regular review of risk‑factor control, ABI measurement and walking capacity prevents progression.

b: Neurogenic claudication (spinal stenosis) – pain worsens with standing, improves with flexion
Musculoskeletal cramp or shin splints – pain not reproducible by fixed distance
Venous claudication – heaviness, swelling, improves with leg elevation
sections.p: Other causes of leg pain can mimic claudication but have different pathophysiology.

b: Non‑compressible arteries in diabetes or chronic kidney disease give ABI >1.30; toe‑brachial index is needed
Doppler waveforms can appear normal in early disease; clinical correlation remains essential
sections.p: Certain measurements may be falsely normal, leading to missed diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rest pain or loss of pulse – possible acute limb ischemia
Chest pain, dyspnoea or neurological deficit suggesting systemic emboli
